strengths: The mean-point correspondence is a simple, original, and potentially useful construction for a difficult camera-geometry problem. Reusing established five-point and P3P solvers makes the approach accessible, while requiring one fewer real correspondence. The manuscript appropriately presents it as an approximate hypothesis generator.

The empirical evaluation is substantial: 90,000 camera triplets across 18 scenes and three datasets, with both PoseLib and GC-RANSAC. Synthetic geometry and noise experiments, outlier tests, threshold sensitivity, and individual-scene results provide meaningful supporting evidence. The supplementary metric also evaluates all three camera pairs.

The paper includes a strengthened five-point baseline, demonstrating benefits beyond comparison with an unrefined implementation. In Table 3, 4p3v(M)+R+F+ENM achieves almost identical PhotoTourism AUC@10 to 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM (76.16 versus 76.20), with lower reported runtime (44.51 versus 56.52 ms). Comparable benefits appear on the other datasets.

Ablations clarify the roles of refinement, filtering, and early non-minimal refitting. Hyperparameters are selected on a held-out scene. The geometric explanation, acknowledgment of approximation error, and supplied code and data archive links support clarity and reproducibility. Together, these merits provide a stronger case for acceptance than rejection.
weaknesses: The runtime comparison with homotopy continuation has a consequential confound. Section 8.3, footnote 8, reports loading its network weights and other data once per RANSAC run, costing approximately 45 ms. This is substantial relative to the reported complete estimation times and could be amortized across triplets. Table 5 actually reports a faster standalone HC solver than either mean-based solver. The evidence therefore does not cleanly establish the claimed speed advantage for repeated estimation.

The strongest speed–accuracy claims exceed the controlled comparisons. Figure 4 omits the fully strengthened five-point baseline included in Tables 2–3. Against that baseline, the best PhotoTourism mean-shift variant improves AUC@10 from 76.20 to 77.14 while increasing runtime from 56.52 to 112.60 ms. This supports a useful trade-off, but leaves its claimed dominance across computational budgets insufficiently established.

Lemma 1 bounds the virtual correspondence's image-space error by the triangle radius, which can be large; it does not bound pose error or establish numerical conditioning. Figure 9 confirms residual approximation error even with noiseless observations. The claim that scene dependence becomes negligible after ENM should therefore be restricted to the evaluated configurations, rather than interpreted as a general reliability guarantee.

There are correctable reporting and reproducibility issues. In Table 7, the Cambridge rows for 4p3v(M)+R+F and 4p3v(M)+R+F+ENM duplicate every reported value of the corresponding affine rows, warranting verification. The manuscript also leaves the exact refinement residual and conversion from the affine fundamental matrix to calibrated poses insufficiently explicit.

strengths: The mean-point correspondence is a simple, original, and useful way to apply established five-point and P3P solvers to the difficult four-point, three-view problem. The contribution is primarily practical, but reducing implementation complexity without training a dedicated solver has clear value for multiview geometry.

The evaluation is substantial: 90,000 camera triplets across 18 scenes and three datasets, with both PoseLib and GC-RANSAC. The supplement includes noise, viewing-angle, depth, outlier, threshold, and component ablations. Evaluation using all three camera pairs also supports the conclusions beyond the main paper's pose metric.

The results demonstrate useful accuracy/runtime alternatives. In Table 3, 4p3v(M)+R+F+ENM achieves essentially the enhanced five-point baseline's PhotoTourism AUC@10 (76.16 versus 76.20) at lower runtime (44.51 versus 56.52 ms). On Aachen, it achieves 57.21 versus 57.11 at 58.08 versus 76.86 ms. These are meaningful practical results even without universal superiority.

The manuscript explains why approximate hypotheses require careful integration with robust estimation. Ablations establish the importance of early refitting and fourth-point refinement, rather than attributing all gains to the centroid heuristic. Held-out parameter validation, implementation settings, and links to source code and archived data support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The runtime comparison against homotopy continuation is materially confounded by initialization. Section 8.3 reports approximately 45 ms for loading its network/data once per RANSAC run, a substantial cost relative to the reported 64.10 ms PhotoTourism runtime. This reusable setup cost should be distinguished from steady-state estimation; the current comparison does not establish an intrinsic speed advantage over that baseline.

The claim of the best speed–accuracy trade-off is stronger than the controlled comparisons establish. Figure 4 does not include the five-point baseline with +R+F, although Table 2 shows these modifications substantially improve it. Against the fully enhanced baseline, the most accurate proposed variant improves PhotoTourism AUC@10 from 76.20 to 77.14 while increasing runtime from 56.52 to 112.60 ms. The evidence supports competitive alternatives more clearly than consistent dominance.

The theoretical justification offers limited predictive control over failures. Lemma 1 bounds the synthetic correspondence's epipolar distance by the triangle's extent, which can greatly exceed the RANSAC threshold; it does not bound recovered pose error or establish convergence of refinement. Figure 9 confirms approximation bias even without measurement noise. The empirical support is valuable, but the statement that scene dependence becomes negligible after ENM should be interpreted only within the tested configurations.

There is a specific reporting concern in Table 7: the Cambridge results for 4p3v(M)+R+F and its +ENM variant exactly duplicate the corresponding affine-method rows across every metric and runtime. This appears to be a correctable table error, but it reduces confidence in those particular ablations. It does not outweigh the broader evidence supporting weak acceptance.

strengths: The mean-point correspondence is a simple, original, and useful construction for approximate four-point, three-view pose estimation. Reusing established five-point and P3P solvers makes the method accessible, while early refitting and refinement provide a coherent way to handle approximation errors.

The practical gains are supported by comparisons with an enhanced baseline. In Table 2, 4p3v(M)+R+F+ENM matches 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM within 0.10 AUC@10 percentage points across all three datasets while reducing reported runtime by approximately 21–31%. The shifted variant achieves the highest aggregate AUC@10 on each dataset.

Evaluation is substantial: 90,000 triplets across 18 scenes, two RANSAC frameworks, synthetic geometry and noise experiments, outlier tests, and component ablations. The supplementary evaluation using the maximum error over all three camera pairs strengthens the evidence beyond the main paper's averaged metric. Parameters are tuned on a separate validation scene.

The manuscript clearly acknowledges that these are approximate hypothesis generators and demonstrates the importance of subsequent optimization. Source-code and archived-data links, together with implementation and evaluation settings, support reproducibility. The useful construction and extensive empirical support favor acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The runtime comparison with HC includes a consequential implementation overhead. Section 8.3 states that HC loads weights/data once per RANSAC invocation, costing approximately 45 ms, while its main reported total runtimes are approximately 60–67 ms. These comparisons do not establish the same speed advantage for applications that retain the loaded model across calls. Table 5 also shows that the basic mean-point solvers themselves are slower than HC per invocation.

The claim of consistently providing the best speed–accuracy trade-off is insufficiently established against the strongest five-point baseline. Figure 4 omits its +R+F variants, although Table 2 shows that these enhancements substantially improve it. Against 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM, the most accurate shifted variant gains only 0.31–0.94 AUC@10 percentage points while taking approximately 1.7–2.0 times longer under early termination. The useful results warrant a more qualified efficiency claim.

The geometric guarantee is limited: Lemma 1 bounds the virtual correspondence's point-to-epipolar-line distance by the triangle's spatial extent. It provides no corresponding pose-error bound or convergence guarantee for refinement, and can be loose for large triangles. Thus, reliability remains primarily empirical; the discussion that scene dependence becomes negligible after ENM is stronger than the analysis establishes.

The evaluation retains only correspondences consistently matched across all three views. However, the five-point baseline requires only three shared triplets and can obtain its remaining two correspondences from a single image pair. The experiments therefore leave its relative practical advantage under partial visibility unresolved, which matters when interpreting the benefit of reducing the sample from five points to four.

strengths: The mean-point correspondence is a simple, original, and useful way to generate four-point three-view pose hypotheses using established five-point and P3P solvers. Avoiding a complicated dedicated polynomial solver gives the contribution clear practical value.

Table 2 demonstrates benefits even against the strengthened five-point baseline. With +R+F+ENM, the mean-point method achieves essentially identical AUC@10 while reducing runtime from 56.52 to 44.51 ms on PhotoTourism and from 47.07 to 32.48 ms on Cambridge. The shifted-mean variant provides additional accuracy at higher computational cost.

The evaluation is substantial: 90,000 triplets across 18 scenes, two RANSAC frameworks, component ablations, noise and outlier experiments, and threshold sensitivity tests. Supplementary evaluation across all three camera pairs addresses the main metric's omission of the second-to-third camera relationship.

The construction and geometric motivation are understandable, and the manuscript explicitly acknowledges approximation errors and dependence on optimization. Code and archived data links, hardware details, and validation of hyperparameters on a withheld scene support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The strongest speed–accuracy claims are not fully established against equally strengthened baselines. Figure 4 omits the five-point +R+F variants reported in Table 2, and the GC-RANSAC comparison also lacks these variants. Against five-point +R+F+ENM, the best shifted-mean variant improves AUC@10 by only 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 percentage points across the three datasets while taking approximately 1.7–2 times longer. These are useful operating points, but do not establish uniformly superior efficiency; uncertainty estimates would also help interpret the smaller gains.

The HC runtime comparison is confounded by initialization overhead. Section 8.3, footnote 8 reports loading model data once per RANSAC run at approximately 45 ms, substantial relative to the reported 60–67 ms total runtimes. Amortized timing with the model already loaded is needed to substantiate the claimed computational advantage over HC.

The theoretical support establishes a correspondence-error bound proportional to triangle size, rather than an informative pose-error or refinement-convergence guarantee. Figure 9 also shows nonzero errors without observation noise. The experiments support effective initialization on the tested distributions, but the claim that ENM makes scene dependence negligible is stronger than this evidence establishes.

There are smaller reporting and reproducibility issues. In Table 7, the Cambridge results for the affine and mean-point methods with +R+F, and with +R+F+ENM, are identical across every reported metric and warrant verification. The conversion from the affine fundamental matrix to calibrated camera poses and the precise refinement objective could also be specified more explicitly. These are correctable issues rather than reasons to dismiss the supported practical contribution.

The strongest shifted-mean variant reaches 77.14, compared with 73.53 for HC. These results support both practical usefulness and improved achievable accuracy.

Matched-time comparisons with that enhanced baseline are needed to substantiate the claimed best trade-off.

The HC timing comparison contains substantial initialization overhead. Section 8.3 reports loading its weights/data once per RANSAC invocation at approximately 45 ms, while Table 2 reports total HC runtimes of approximately 60–67 ms. strengths: The mean-point correspondence is a simple, original, and useful way to construct approximate four-point, three-view pose hypotheses using mature five-point and P3P solvers. Its practical value comes from making a difficult geometric estimation problem accessible without a specialized learned solver.

The results demonstrate useful performance against a strengthened conventional baseline. In Table 3, 4p3v(M)+R+F+ENM achieves essentially the same PhotoTourism AUC@10 as 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM (76.16 versus 76.20), with lower reported runtime (44.51 versus 56.52 ms). The shifted-mean variant achieves the highest accuracy across all three datasets, albeit with additional computation.

The evaluation is substantial: 90,000 triplets across 18 scenes, two RANSAC frameworks, synthetic geometry and noise experiments, and threshold and outlier sensitivity studies. The supplementary evaluation using errors across all three camera pairs addresses the main metric's omission of the second-to-third camera relationship.

The ablations establish the importance of refinement, filtering, and early non-minimal refitting, while honestly exposing the poor performance of the unmodified affine solver. Held-out parameter validation, specified implementation settings, and links to archived code and data support reproducibility. Together, these merits provide a stronger case for acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The runtime comparison with the homotopy baseline has a material confound. Section 8.3, footnote 8, reports approximately 45 ms for loading its weights/data once per RANSAC run, which is substantial relative to the reported 60–67 ms overall runtimes. Such initialization can be amortized across triplets. The reported timings therefore do not establish a general speed advantage over an initialized HC implementation.

The claim of consistently superior speed–accuracy trade-offs is stronger than the comparison supports. Figure 4 omits the enhanced 5pt+P3P+R+F baselines, although Tables 2–3 show that these enhancements recover much of the accuracy gap. Against the fully enhanced baseline, the best shifted-mean variant improves AUC@10 by 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 percentage points across the three datasets while taking approximately 1.7–2 times longer under early termination.

The theoretical justification establishes only a loose correspondence-error bound. Lemma 1 bounds the synthetic point's distance to an epipolar line by triangle size; it does not bound pose error or establish stability near degenerate configurations. Thus, it cannot by itself justify comparisons with competing methods' pose failures, and the statement that ENM makes scene dependence negligible should remain qualified by the tested configurations.

A localized reporting issue reduces confidence in part of the supplementary ablation: Table 7 gives identical Cambridge metrics and runtimes for the A and M variants with +R+F, and again with +R+F+ENM. These appear potentially duplicated and need clarification. This concern affects those specific comparisons rather than the broader experimental contribution.

strengths: The mean-point correspondence is an original, simple, and useful construction for a difficult geometric vision problem. Combining it with established five-point and P3P solvers provides an accessible alternative to substantially more complex three-view solvers. The contribution is valuable as a practical approximate estimator.

The results demonstrate useful gains even against the improved five-point baseline. In Table 3, 4p3v(M)+R+F+ENM achieves nearly identical PhotoTourism AUC@10 to 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM (76.16 versus 76.20), while reducing runtime from 56.52 to 44.51 ms. On Cambridge, both achieve 66.31, with runtimes of 32.48 versus 47.07 ms.

The evaluation is substantial: 90,000 triplets across 18 scenes and three datasets, with both PoseLib and GC-RANSAC. Synthetic geometry and noise experiments, component ablations, threshold sensitivity, outlier experiments, and an alternative metric covering all camera pairs provide meaningful support for the complete pipeline.

The manuscript clearly explains the approximations and the roles of refitting, refinement, and filtering. Hyperparameter selection uses a held-out scene, and code and data archive links support reproducibility. Reporting the poor performance of unrefined affine estimates and the lack of superiority in two-view estimation helps establish the contribution's practical scope.
weaknesses: The claim of consistently achieving the best speed–accuracy trade-off is incompletely supported against the strongest baseline. Figure 4 omits the +R+F-enhanced five-point baseline included in Tables 2–3; that baseline is also absent from the GC-RANSAC comparison. In Table 3, the fully enhanced shifted-mean solver improves PhotoTourism AUC@10 from 76.20 to 77.14 but takes 112.60 versus 56.52 ms. Curves comparing equally enhanced methods at matched runtimes are needed to establish the stronger efficiency claim.

The homotopy baseline's timing includes an avoidable initialization cost: Section 8.3, footnote 8, reports loading network data once per RANSAC call, taking approximately 45 ms. Applications processing multiple triplets could amortize this cost. Consequently, the reported RANSAC speed advantage over HC does not establish an advantage with initialization amortized. Table 5 actually reports lower standalone runtime for HC than for the unshifted mean solver (66.06 versus 83.92 microseconds).

The theoretical support has limited scope. Lemma 1 bounds the virtual correspondence's epipolar distance by a potentially large centroid-to-vertex distance; it does not bound pose error or establish convergence of refinement. Figure 9 also shows nonzero errors on noiseless inputs. The assertion that scene dependence becomes negligible after ENM therefore remains an empirical observation within the tested regimes.

A correctable reporting issue warrants verification: in the Cambridge portion of Table 7, the +R+F and +R+F+ENM rows repeat all accuracy statistics and runtimes between the affine and unshifted mean methods. These apparent duplicated entries reduce confidence in those particular comparisons.

strengths: The mean-point correspondence construction provides a useful, original practical approach to three-camera pose estimation. Reusing established five-point and P3P solvers makes the method straightforward to implement without requiring a complicated dedicated polynomial solver.

The empirical support is substantial: 90,000 triplets across 18 scenes and three datasets, evaluation in both PoseLib and GC-RANSAC, and supplementary experiments covering noise, outliers, geometry, thresholds, and individual components. The alternative metric covering all three camera pairs strengthens the evaluation.

The results demonstrate useful tradeoffs even against an enhanced baseline. In Tables 2–3, 4p3v(M)+R+F+ENM achieves essentially identical PhotoTourism AUC@10 to 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM (76.16 versus 76.20), while reducing runtime from 56.52 to 44.51 ms. Comparable benefits appear on Cambridge and Aachen.

The manuscript clearly acknowledges that its solvers are approximate and investigates the refinement needed to make them practical. Parameter validation on a separate scene, detailed ablations, and provided code and data archive links support reproducibility. These practical contributions and supporting experiments favor weak acceptance.
weaknesses: The runtime comparison with the homotopy solver is materially confounded by initialization overhead. Section 8.3, footnote 8, states that approximately 45 ms of loading occurs once per RANSAC run. Such loading could be amortized across triplets in a persistent application. Table 5 actually reports lower standalone runtime for HC than either mean-point variant, so claims of speed superiority require qualification.

The strongest accuracy gains over the enhanced five-point baseline are modest and expensive. On PhotoTourism, the fully enhanced delta variant improves AUC@10 from 76.20 to 77.14 while increasing runtime from 56.52 to 112.60 ms. Moreover, Figure 4 and the GC-RANSAC comparison omit the baseline's +R/+F variants, despite their inclusion in Tables 2–3. Consequently, consistently superior accuracy–runtime tradeoffs against the strongest baseline are not fully established.

The theoretical justification establishes only a loose image-space bound. Lemma 1 bounds correspondence-to-epipolar-line distance by triangle size; it does not bound pose error or establish when refinement will recover a useful solution. Figure 9 shows residual errors even with noiseless correspondences. The empirical results support practical robustness, but the claim that scene dependence becomes negligible is stronger than the analysis establishes.

A smaller reporting concern appears in Table 7: the Cambridge results repeat every metric and runtime for the affine and mean-point +R+F variants, and again for their +ENM variants. These unexplained identical rows reduce confidence in that particular comparison, although they do not invalidate the independent main-table evidence.
